extracted.intended_audience: federal judges, patent litigators, and juries (users of model jury instructions)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent litigation issues including infringement theories (e.g., inducement, §271(f)(2), §271(g)) and invalidity defenses (prior art, anticipation, public use, on-sale bar, experimental use, printed publication, prior invention). Intended to guide judges in instructing juries and to identify factual issues for jury findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staple article / substantial non-infringing use
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use' is something that has uses other than as a part or component of the patented product/other than in the patented method, and those other uses are not occasional, farfetched, impractical, or experimental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the accused component has substantial non-infringing uses — uses that are regular and realistic rather than occasional, farfetched, impractical, or experimental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful blindness evidence for knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant]’s knowledge that the component was especially made or adapted for use in an infringing product/method may be shown with evidence of willful blindness where [the Defendant] consciously ignored the existence of both the patent and direct infringement of that patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To find willful blindness: (1) [the Defendant] must have subjectively believed there was a high probability that a patent existed covering the accused product/method, and (2) [the Defendant] must have taken deliberate actions to avoid learning of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 271(f)(2) infringement elements (supply abroad)
rubrics_metrics.description: [To show infringement under Section 271(f)(2), the Plaintiff must prove each of the following by a preponderance of the evidence:] (1) [the Defendant] actually supplied the components from the United States into a foreign country or caused them to be supplied from the United States to a foreign country; (2) [the Defendant] knew or should have known that the components were especially made or adapted for use in a product that infringes a claim of the patent; (3) those components have no substantial non-infringing use; and (4) [the Defendant] intended for the components to be combined into that product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that the components actually were combined into an infringing product — it suffices that the defendant intended for them to be combined into a product that would have infringed if combined in the United States. In this context, a 'substantial use' is one that is not occasional, farfetched, impractical, experimental, or hypothetical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'substantial use' (§ 271(f)(2) context)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the context of Section 271(f)(2), a substantial use of an accused feature is one that is not occasional, farfetched, impractical, experimental, or hypothetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether non-infringing uses are substantial (regular, significant) rather than incidental or unrealistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 271(g) infringement elements (product made by patented process)
rubrics_metrics.description: [To show infringement under Section 271(g), the Plaintiff must prove that:] (1) the Defendant imported into the United States or, within the United States, sold/offered for sale/used a product that was made by a process that includes all steps of at least one claim of the patent; (2) the product was made between [issue date of patent] and [expiration date of patent/date of trial]; and (3) the Defendant imported/sold/offered for sale/used the product between [issue date] and [expiration date/date of trial].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must decide whether the evidence establishes the product was 'made by' the claimed process. If the product was materially changed by later processes or is a trivial/non-essential part of another product, you must find it was not 'made by' the claimed process. Infringement under §271(g) does not require a single entity to perform the patented process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary rule: Defendant's burden to prove invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The burden of proof for invalidity is clear and convincing evidence for each claim alleged invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (pre-AIA) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes any item received into evidence that: (1) any product/method publicly known or used by others in the United States before the claimed invention was invented; (2) any product/method in public use or on sale in the United States before the Cutoff Date; (3) any patents that issued before the Cutoff Date; (4) any publications having dates of public accessibility before the Cutoff Date; and (5) any product/method made by anyone in the United States before the date of invention where the claimed invention was not later abandoned, suppressed, or concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and list prior art admitted into evidence and instruct the jury on factual issues (date, public availability, etc.) relevant to prior art status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (AIA) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes anything patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public anywhere in the world before the effective filing date of the claim(s); and anything described in a patent or application published or deemed published naming another inventor and filed before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply AIA definitions of effective filing date (35 U.S.C. §100(i)) and recognize statutory exceptions as instructed elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to prior art (grace period and derived disclosures)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure made one year or less before the effective filing date shall not be prior art if: (A) the disclosure was made by the inventor or joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from such inventor; or (B) the subject matter disclosed had, before such disclosure, been publicly disclosed by the inventor or another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from such inventor. Also, a disclosure shall not be prior art if the subject matter was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor, or the subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If factual issues exist about disclosure timing or ownership, identify them to the jury and instruct regarding §102 exceptions under AIA as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of whether prior art was considered by the PTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether a particular prior art reference was considered by the Patent Examiner during prosecution, the Defendant must prove invalidity by clear and convincing evidence; the burden never changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the PTO did not have all material facts, its considered judgment may lose force; evidence that is materially new may make the challenger’s burden easier to sustain. A jury instruction on the effect of new evidence can and when requested most often should be given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity of independent and dependent claims (claim-by-claim evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent claim does not refer to any other claim. A dependent claim refers to at least one other claim and includes all elements of the claim to which it refers plus additional elements. You must evaluate the invalidity of each asserted claim separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an independent claim is invalid, dependent claims are not automatically invalid — decide validity claim-by-claim. (Text also states: if you find a dependent claim is invalid, you must find the independent claim from which it depends is also invalid.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of invalidity of a patent claim is determined from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in the field of the claimed invention as of the time of the invention/effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use POSITA's knowledge and understanding at the relevant time when assessing prior art, enablement, and obviousness-related factual inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (newness) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove anticipation, the Defendant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the claimed invention is not new. To anticipate a claim, each element in the claim must be present in a single item of prior art and arranged or combined in the same way as recited in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may not combine two or more items of prior art to find anticipation. Consider what a POSITA would have understood from review of the particular prior art reference. If inherency is alleged, instruct on inherency requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency in anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art inherently anticipates if the missing element(s) or feature(s) would necessarily result from what the single item of prior art teaches to a POSITA. A party claiming inherent anticipation must prove that the allegedly inherent element(s) necessarily are present by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence outside the prior art reference (including experimental testing) may be used to show inherent elements. It is not required that a POSITA recognized the inherent disclosure at the time; likelihood is insufficient — the element must necessarily have existed or resulted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public knowledge (pre-AIA) as invalidating
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention defined was publicly known by others in the United States before it was invented by the patentee (pre-AIA §102(a) standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is a factual dispute about date of invention or priority, instruct jury how to determine the Cutoff Date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public availability (AIA §102(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the claimed invention was available to the public before the effective filing date of the claim (AIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If factual issues exist about disclosures within the one-year grace period or derived disclosures, instruct the jury regarding §102(b) and (c) exceptions as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public use (pre-AIA) definition and factors
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was publicly used by others in the United States before the invention date or was publicly used in the U.S. more than one year before the U.S. filing date. An invention was publicly used in the U.S. if an embodiment was both (1) accessible to the public or commercially exploited in the United States, and (2) ready for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors relevant: nature of the activity, public access to the use, confidentiality obligations, commercial exploitation (even if specifics kept secret), circumstances of testing/experimentation. Absence of affirmative steps to conceal is evidence of public use; secret third-party use is not public unless members of public or employees had access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public use (AIA) worldwide standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Under AIA, a claim is invalid if the claimed invention was in public use anywhere in the world before the effective filing date. An invention was in public use if accessible to the public or commercially exploited anywhere in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial exploitation includes selling or promoting a product made using the invention even if the specifics were kept secret. To be public use, the invention also must have been ready for patenting at the time (reduced to practice or described sufficiently).

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if before the cutoff an embodiment of the claimed invention was both (1) the subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale (pre-AIA: in the United States), and (2) ready for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commercial offer for sale exists if another party could make a binding contract by accepting the offer. An offer for sale even if confidential can trigger the bar. It is not required that a sale was made or that the sale terms disclosed invention details. Ready for patenting requires reduction to practice or sufficiently specific descriptions enabling a POSITA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception to public use/on-sale
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain activities are experimental if they are a legitimate effort to test claimed features of the invention or to determine if the invention will work for its intended purpose. So long as the primary purpose is experimentation, it does not matter that the public used the invention or that the inventor incidentally derived profit from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only experimentation by or under the control of the inventor (or assignee) qualifies; experimentation by a third party for its own purposes does not. The experimentation must relate to claimed features and be for technological improvement, not primarily for commercial exploitation. If plaintiff produces strong experimental-use evidence, the jury may find no prior public use or sale despite defendant's proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if a printed publication described the invention before the effective filing date/date of invention/more than one year before application. A printed publication is maintained in some tangible form and must have been sufficiently accessible to persons interested in the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility means distributed or otherwise made available such that persons interested and ordinarily skilled exercising reasonable diligence could locate it. The disclosure must be enabling enough for a POSITA to use the invention without undue experimentation. Issued patents and published patent applications qualify as printed publications as of their publication dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior invention (pre-AIA) defense
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was invented by another person in the United States before the patentee (pre-AIA). The Defendant must show by clear and convincing evidence that (1) before the patentee the third party reduced to practice a product/method that included all the claim features, or (2) the third party was first to conceive and exercised reasonable diligence in reducing to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additionally, the third party's product/method must have been sufficiently developed that one skilled in the art would have recognized it would work for its intended purpose. This defense may be negated if the invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed.
